description: Team from Mérida, Yucatán, on the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge. K’áak’ means “fire” in Yucatec Maya. Every spring our peninsula burns: satellites detect tens of thousands of hotspots a year, but two sensor generations can’t be compared directly. We’re building one consistent fire calendar from 25 years of satellite records. Skills: data analysis, anomaly detection, dashboards, cybersecurity.
summary: In Yucatán, burning to plant the milpa is legal and each municipality must authorize burns, but it does so without data. Using VIIRS fire detections since 2012, we found that, in the places where fire recurs, the four weeks with the most fire in their past catch 49 % of the next season's fire, against 23 % for the official burning window. K'áak' (Yucatec Maya for "fire") is a free website that gives each municipality of the Yucatán Peninsula a fire calendar built from 25 years of NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire detections: where fire returns, in which weeks it burns, and whether this season runs above or below normal, so Civil Protection knows where to go and when to watch. MODIS on Aqua, which carries most of the record before 2012, sees three to five times less fire than VIIRS, so the raw record seems to triple around 2012, when only the sensor changed. We calibrate MODIS to the VIIRS scale with a factor for each zone and time of year and check the result with pass/fail rules fixed in code before computing the results, plus a comparison with CONAFOR's ground records.
details:
What it does. K'áak' is a free website, in English and Spanish, that turns 25 years of satellite fire detections into a fire calendar for each municipality of the Yucatán Peninsula (127 on the map; three recent ones have no official boundary yet, so their fire counts in the municipality they split from). The area of interest is the municipality, because by law it is the authority that approves burns: a user types its name, taps it on the map or shares their location. They then see where fire returns almost every year (each place links to Google Maps so a crew can find it), in which weeks it burns in a normal year, with its peak week and, in Yucatán, its zone's official burning window, and how the current season compares with a normal year, the median of 2001 to 2025. Each municipality has a one-page sheet that a community leader can forward by messaging app, and the data behind the municipality charts, the almanac and the full series downloads as CSV.

Why it matters. Burning to plant the milpa is legal and regulated in Yucatán: the state agriculture ministry (SEDER) sets burning windows by zone, and each municipality must authorize burns and report at the end of the season. Today it does so without data. We measured how well a calendar learned from the past works: in the places where fire recurs (1 km cells with fire in at least 30 % of earlier years), we took the four weeks with the most fire in their previous years (VIIRS data since 2012), and from 2019 to 2025 those weeks caught 49 % of the next season's fire there, against 23 % for SEDER's current official window. The window says when burning is allowed, not when it happens, so this is not a fault of SEDER; it shows when it is worth watching. Smoke also reaches the cities: on 14 May 2024, Mérida was among the five most polluted cities in Mexico because of fires in the previous days.

How the harmonization works.

1. We take every MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP and NOAA-20) detection over the peninsula from NASA FIRMS since 2001 and assign each to its municipality.

2. We count fire on a common grid of about 1 km per day, so that several detections of one fire count once, with one satellite per period: Terra until July 2002, then Aqua, then Suomi NPP from 2012, with NOAA-20 filling the days Suomi NPP sent no data.

3. We calibrate MODIS to the VIIRS scale on 2013 to 2020, when both fly together, with a separate factor for each zone (SEDER's four burning zones in Yucatán, Campeche and Quintana Roo) and time of year (2.8 to 5.3 for Aqua; 4.0 to 9.7 for Terra, which flew alone until July 2002), because one factor does not fit: among CONAFOR's recorded wildfires, Suomi NPP detects 3.5 times as many of the small ones as MODIS does, but only 1.2 times as many of those larger than 100 ha, most of which MODIS already sees.

4. We validate with pass/fail rules fixed in code (pipeline/validar.py) before computing the results. The false jump of 2012 disappears (×3.26 before calibration, ×0.90 after); since 2013 to 2015 are among the calibration years, we reran it with factors calibrated only on 2016 to 2020, and it gives ×0.91, against ×0.90 with the current factors; the factor holds on the Aqua years 2021 to 2025, which the calibration did not use; and NOAA-20 can carry the series on (between 0.99 and 1.03 NOAA-20 hot spots per Suomi NPP hot spot each year from 2019 to 2025), which matters now that Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026. In an informative comparison with CONAFOR's ground records of forest fires, Suomi NPP sees 53 % of 1,222 recorded fires, against 9 % expected by chance, and 84 % of those larger than 100 ha.

5. A scheduled job downloads new detections from the FIRMS API four times a day, and the site recomputes the current season.

One assumption cannot be tested directly: before 2012 only MODIS flew, so we assume the factor measured from 2013 to 2020 also holds for 2001 to 2011. Two indirect checks support it: Aqua's median fire radiative power from March to May barely changed (29.9 MW in 2003–2011, 29.1 MW in 2013–2020), and a curve instead of a constant factor does not reduce the error when each year is left out. For a single municipality, an old Aqua year can be about 20 % off (about 8 % for a whole zone, and about 45 % for the Terra years 2001–2002), so the long series is solid for zones and the state, and a reference for one municipality in one old year. The site draws those years as striped bars, so nobody reads them as measured by VIIRS.

Why day by day, and why March to May. SEDER sets the allowed burning windows by date, so the site shows the calendar day by day; the almanac shows each month and the downloadable series each week. The comparison with normal covers the burning season, March to May. Outside it, 119 of the 127 municipalities have a median of zero hot spots in the first half of November, so comparing the current month would say nothing.

What we have not done yet. Nobody from Civil Protection or SEDER has used the site yet; the next step is to show the sheets of two municipalities to their Civil Protection offices before the 2027 season. The site shows the 49 % against 23 % result on its Burn window page, but not yet the four weeks of each place where fire recurs. The area of interest is fixed to the municipality: drawing a free area or choosing any range of dates is not built. The method only needs FIRMS detections, a map of local administrative units and the years when MODIS and VIIRS overlap, which exist for any region, but we have only run it on the peninsula.

What it does not do. K'áak' does not predict fires and does not send alerts; NASA FIRMS already sends free fire alerts. A satellite does not see every fire, and no detections does not mean no fire. A detection outside the allowed dates is a question for SEDER and Civil Protection, not proof of an illegal burn. 2026 was the calmest season since 2001 in Yucatán and 2025 the second calmest, so we do not claim that fire is increasing.

Tools. Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Shapely, PyArrow) for the data; a static site in HTML, CSS and JavaScript over a cloud-free VIIRS mosaic from NASA GIBS, hosted on Cloudflare Pages; GitHub Actions for tests and the scheduled update; Playwright and axe-core to test the site in both languages, including accessibility.

Code and data: https://github.com/Ghosflot/kaak-yucatan (Apache 2.0). Every figure is traced to its source in the repository (docs/01, docs/02 and the README).
